title: Want + obstacle = story
rule: A story needs someone who wants something, and something in the way.

examples.work: I wanted to leave by six for my cousin's engagement. At 5:45, my manager called a meeting.
examples.everyday: I wanted one quiet chai before work. Then the milk boiled over and the gas ran out.

insteadOf: I left at six and went to my cousin's engagement.
analogy: A run chase is exciting only because the bowler is trying to stop you.
tryPrompt: Think of today. What did you want, and what got in the way? Say it in two sentences.

lesson.title: A want and something in the way

title: A list of events is a report
rule: If nothing gets in the way, you're giving a report, not telling a story.

examples.work: We were sure the review would go well. Ten minutes in, the VP asked why repeat users had dropped. Nobody had checked.
examples.everyday: I took the 8:10 metro like always. Today it stopped between stations for twenty minutes, and I walked in at 9:40.

insteadOf: We had the review, we showed the numbers, and it finished at six.
analogy: A timetable lists the stops. A story is the day the train stops between them.
tryPrompt: Tell yesterday as a report in one line. Now add the one thing that went wrong.
credit: The Moth (storytelling tips): without something to gain or lose, it's an essay

lesson.title: A want and something in the way

title: Small trouble is enough
rule: The problem can be small and ordinary, as long as it matters to you.

examples.work: I needed the projector for my ten o'clock demo, and the HDMI cable was missing.
examples.everyday: I promised Amma I'd bring coriander. The shop had sold out by seven.

insteadOf: It was the worst day of my life. Everything collapsed.
analogy: A last-over finish in a gully match is still thrilling.
tryPrompt: Find one small problem from this week, like a late cab or a missing file. Say what you wanted and what stopped you.

lesson.title: A want and something in the way

title: The obstacle can be you
rule: Your own mistake can be the thing that gets in the way.

examples.work: I wanted to send the report by noon. Then I realised I'd emailed it to the wrong Rahul.
examples.everyday: I wanted to surprise my sister on her birthday. Then I posted the cake photo in the family WhatsApp group. She's in it.

insteadOf: The team was slow, IT was slow, and the client changed everything.
analogy: Sometimes the batter runs himself out. That's still a story worth telling.
tryPrompt: Think of a small mistake you made this month. Say what you wanted, then how you got in your own way.

lesson.title: A want and something in the way

title: "I wanted…", "I was trying to…"
rule: Show the want with "I wanted to" or "I was trying to".

examples.work: I was trying to leave by six, but at 5:45 my manager called a meeting.
examples.everyday: I wanted to watch the match in peace, but my nephew wanted the TV for cartoons.

insteadOf: I am wanting to leave early, but the meeting started.
analogy: Like setting the destination in Google Maps before the road closes.
tryPrompt: Start a story about today with "I was trying to…". Then say what stopped you.

lesson.title: A want and something in the way

title: "And then" makes a list
rule: A chain of "and then" sounds like a list, so listeners drift off.

examples.work: I reached office early, but the client called, furious. So I rewrote the deck before ten.
examples.everyday: We left for Mysore at six, but the car broke down near Ramanagara. So we had idli at a roadside stall and waited for the mechanic.

insteadOf: I reached office, and then the meeting started, and then the client called.
analogy: A list is a queue at the bank. A story is the queue where someone cuts in.
tryPrompt: Tell your morning with "and then" three times. Now say it again with one "but" and one "so".
credit: South Park writers' "but / therefore" rule, built into Randy Olson's ABT

title: "But" brings the problem
rule: Use "but" at the moment things stop going to plan.

examples.work: The demo was at three, but at 2:55 the Wi-Fi went down.
examples.everyday: I booked a table for Riya's birthday, but the restaurant had lost our booking.

insteadOf: The demo was at three, and the Wi-Fi went down.
analogy: "But" is the googly: the ball looked straight, then it turned.
tryPrompt: Finish this with a "but": "I left home early today…" Then do one from your own day.
credit: South Park writers' "but / therefore" rule, built into Randy Olson's ABT

title: "So" shows what you did next
rule: After the problem, use "so" to show what you did because of it.

examples.work: The Wi-Fi went down, so I ran the demo from my phone's hotspot.
examples.everyday: The restaurant lost our booking, so we ordered biryani and ate on Riya's terrace.

insteadOf: The Wi-Fi went down. Then I called IT. Then I used my phone.
analogy: Rain stops play, so the captain changes the plan. That change is the story.
tryPrompt: Think of one problem from this week. Say it with "but", then what you did with "so".

title: The three-part story
rule: A short story fits in three parts: what happened, "but…", "so…".

examples.work: I had a client call at nine, but my laptop wouldn't start. So I joined from my manager's laptop.
examples.everyday: I went to buy milk, but the kirana was shut for Onam. So I walked to the big store and came back with three bags of snacks.

insteadOf: So many things happened today, the cab, the meeting, the rain, everything.
analogy: Like making chai: boil the water, add the tea, add the milk. Three steps, done.
tryPrompt: Tell one moment from today in three sentences. Start the second with "but" and the third with "so".

title: Lean on "but" and "so" aloud
rule: Say "but" and "so" clearly when speaking, because they carry the turns.

examples.work: We planned to launch on Monday. But testing found a bug. So we moved it to Wednesday.
examples.everyday: We planned a picnic at Lalbagh. But it poured all morning. So we had the picnic on the living-room floor.

insteadOf: So, basically, and then the thing happened, and then…
analogy: Like indicators on a car: they tell people behind you that you're turning.
tryPrompt: Say your three-part story aloud. Hit "but" and "so" a little harder than the other words.

title: Pick one moment
rule: Asked about your day? Pick one moment and tell just that.

examples.work: Best part of today? My manager used my slide to open the team meeting.
examples.everyday: Funniest moment today? My four-year-old niece told the delivery man our full address, PIN code included.

insteadOf: I woke up, had chai, took the bus, reached office, had meetings, came home.
analogy: Show one great photo, not the whole wedding album.
tryPrompt: What's one moment from today you'd tell a friend? Say just that moment in two sentences.

lesson.title: One moment, not the whole day

title: Choose the surprising moment
rule: Pick the moment that surprised, annoyed or amused you most.

examples.work: Today an intern on her second day found a bug our team had missed for a year.
examples.everyday: My auto driver refused UPI. Then he asked if I had change for a five-hundred note.

insteadOf: Today was okay. Normal day, meetings, lunch, nothing much.
analogy: Out of a whole thali, you remember the one dish that was too spicy.
tryPrompt: Name three moments from today. Pick the one that surprised you most and tell only that.

lesson.title: One moment, not the whole day

title: Skip the timeline
rule: Leave out the steps before the moment and start close to it.

examples.work: Just before my demo, my laptop showed a blue screen.
examples.everyday: On the way home, the metro stopped between stations, and a stranger started singing old Kishore Kumar songs.

insteadOf: I woke up at seven, had chai, took the metro, reached office, opened my laptop…
analogy: Match highlights skip the dot balls and go straight to the wickets.
tryPrompt: Think of today's moment. What's the last thing that happened just before it? Start there.

lesson.title: One moment, not the whole day

title: Thirty seconds is plenty
rule: When someone asks about your day, aim for about thirty seconds.

examples.work: Today a client said our app was "too easy to use". He meant it as a complaint.
examples.everyday: My mother learnt to send voice notes today. I've received eleven since lunch.

insteadOf: Okay, so, long story, let me start from Monday…
analogy: Like a T20 innings: short, sharp, and nobody checks the clock.
tryPrompt: Tell today's moment aloud and time it. Under 30 seconds? Good. Over? Cut the start.

lesson.title: One moment, not the whole day

title: Catch one moment each night
rule: Each night, note the one moment from today you'd tell a friend.

examples.work: Moment: Priya from finance laughed at my joke in the stand-up. First time in six months.
examples.everyday: Moment: my dad asked me how to use Google Maps, then told me I was going the wrong way.

insteadOf: Nothing happened today. My days are all the same.
analogy: Like saving one photo a day. In a month, you have an album.
tryPrompt: Tonight, write one line: the moment from today you'd tell a friend. Just the moment, not the story.

lesson.title: One moment, not the whole day

title: A story is a change
rule: A story shows something changing, not just things happening.

examples.work: I walked into that review sure I'd be praised. I walked out knowing I'd never once asked the client what they wanted.
examples.everyday: I sat down to teach my nephew chess. Twenty minutes later, he was teaching me.

insteadOf: I went to the review, they asked questions, I answered, and it ended at six.
analogy: A photo of the stumps standing is boring. A photo of them flying is a story.
tryPrompt: Think of something you see differently now than a year ago. What made it change?
credit: Matthew Dicks (Storyworthy); The Moth: a story shows change

title: The five-second moment
rule: Find the few seconds where you changed or understood something new.

examples.work: Our intern said users don't scroll that far. I almost told her to wait. Then I realised she was right.
examples.everyday: My niece asked why I check my phone at dinner. I had no answer, so I put the phone in the other room.

insteadOf: So I learned that listening is important for leaders.
analogy: Like the one ball that turns a match: everything before builds to it.
tryPrompt: Think of a time you realised something. What were the few seconds when it clicked? Describe just those.

title: Small changes count
rule: The change can be tiny, like a new habit or a new opinion.

examples.work: I used to answer emails during meetings. Then I missed my own name being called. Now my laptop stays shut.
examples.everyday: I always thought I hated karela. Then my friend Fatima's mother made it with jaggery. Now I ask for it.

insteadOf: Nothing big has ever happened to me, so I have no stories.
analogy: One pinch of salt changes the whole dal.
tryPrompt: Name one small thing you do differently now. Tell the moment that made you start.

title: "I realised…" is a change too
rule: Understanding something new counts as a change, even if nothing else moves.

examples.work: Halfway through my answer, I realised the client had never asked about features. He'd asked about the launch date.
examples.everyday: Watching my dad fix the tap, I realised he'd been doing these jobs quietly for thirty years.

insteadOf: So the meeting ended, and I went back to my desk.
analogy: Like a light coming on in a dark room: nothing moves, but now you see everything.
tryPrompt: Finish this about your week: "And right there, I realised…" Then tell what led up to it.

title: Say the change in one line
rule: End by saying what's different now, in one short line.

examples.work: I lost a day's work in a power cut because I hadn't saved. Now I save every few minutes.
examples.everyday: I got lost in Pune because I trusted my memory over Google Maps. Now I check the map before I leave, even for places I know.

insteadOf: So yeah, I learned many things about many things, that's it.
analogy: The last line is the scoreboard: it tells everyone how the match ended.
tryPrompt: Tell a small mistake from this month. End with one line that starts "Now I…".

title: Start in the action
rule: Open with the moment things happen, not the weather or the date.

examples.work: The fire alarm went off one minute into my first client demo.
examples.everyday: The cooker whistle shot off and hit the ceiling just as our guests rang the bell.

insteadOf: So yesterday was a normal Tuesday, I woke up at seven…
analogy: A good film doesn't show the hero brushing his teeth, unless the toothbrush matters.
tryPrompt: Take today's moment. Say your first line so that it starts with something happening.
credit: The Moth (a first line that grabs attention); Matthew Dicks (Storyworthy)

lesson.title: Start in the action, end clean

title: Drop "So yesterday…"
rule: Cut the warm-up words and say your first real sentence straight away.

examples.work: Yesterday I almost got told off for being too helpful.
examples.everyday: Last night, my grandmother beat me at Ludo four times in a row.

insteadOf: So, basically, yesterday something happened at work, okay, so…
analogy: Skip the long run-up. Just bowl.
tryPrompt: Say your opening line for today's moment. Start with what happened, not with "so" or "basically".

lesson.title: Start in the action, end clean

title: Know your last line first
rule: Before you start, decide the exact line you'll finish on.

examples.work: I sent my manager "Quick question?" at 6 p.m. She called back, worried something was on fire. It was about font size. That's the day I stopped writing "quick question".
examples.everyday: My friends dared me to order in Tamil at a Chennai restaurant. I asked for two coffees and got two plates of pongal. Now I just point.

insteadOf: …and then, yeah, so, anyway, that was the whole thing, I guess.
analogy: A cab driver who knows the address drives straight. One who doesn't goes in circles.
tryPrompt: Pick today's moment. Before telling it, say your last line out loud. Then tell it and land there.
credit: The Moth (know your last line); Matthew Dicks (build the story from its end)

lesson.title: Start in the action, end clean

title: Stop after the last line
rule: Say your last line and stop, with no "so yeah, that's it".

examples.work: I spent all weekend fixing the bug. On Monday, the client said they liked it the old way.
examples.everyday: My dad finally learnt to video call. Now he calls during every match to show me his TV.

insteadOf: …and the client said they liked it the old way. So yeah, that's it, crazy, right?
analogy: When the batter hits the winning run, he doesn't keep running.
tryPrompt: Tell today's moment. The second your last line is out, stop talking and smile.

lesson.title: Start in the action, end clean

title: Pick one tense and stay in it
rule: Tell the whole scene in past tense, or the whole scene in present.

examples.work: I walked in, and my manager looked at the clock. Then she smiled and said, "Coffee's on you."
examples.everyday: I'm on the bus. The conductor looks at my ticket. He shakes his head and points at the date.

insteadOf: I walk in and my manager looked at me and says, "You're late."
analogy: Like driving on the left: switch sides halfway and everyone gets confused.
tryPrompt: Tell today's moment in past tense. Then tell it again in present. Don't mix the two.

lesson.title: Start in the action, end clean

title: Name the exact thing
rule: Swap a general word for the exact one: not "vehicle", "Activa".

examples.work: I rode my Activa to the office and ate a cold masala dosa at my desk.
examples.everyday: We went for a drive in my uncle's old Maruti 800 and stopped for Maggi.

insteadOf: I took my vehicle to the office and had some food at my desk.
analogy: "Food was nice" tells me nothing. "Smoky dal with garlic tadka" makes me hungry.
tryPrompt: Say one sentence about your lunch today. Now say it again with the exact names of things.
credit: Chip & Dan Heath, Made to Stick (Concrete)

title: Describe it, don't judge it
rule: Instead of "bad" or "nice", say what actually happened.

examples.work: By slide four, half the team had switched their cameras off.
examples.everyday: We sat on Silk Board flyover for forty minutes. The auto driver switched off the engine to save petrol.

insteadOf: The meeting was really boring.
analogy: Don't say the biryani was good. Say you went back for thirds.
tryPrompt: Think of something today you'd call "bad" or "nice". Say what actually happened instead.
credit: Chip & Dan Heath, Made to Stick (Concrete)

title: A number makes it real
rule: Use a real number instead of "many", "a lot" or "very".

examples.work: The client sent 37 changes at 11:40 p.m., the night before launch.
examples.everyday: My aunt sent 14 good-morning messages to the family group before eight.

insteadOf: The client sent a lot of changes, very late.
analogy: "He scored a lot" is forgotten by lunch. "He scored 183" is remembered for years.
tryPrompt: Find one "a lot" or "very" in your day. Swap it for a real number.
credit: Chip & Dan Heath, Made to Stick (Concrete)

title: The detail only you noticed
rule: Add one small detail that only someone who was there would know.

examples.work: When I got in, the office was empty, except for the cleaner watching cricket on his phone.
examples.everyday: The wedding hall was packed, and one uncle was asleep in the front row, still holding his plate.

insteadOf: The office was empty when I got in.
analogy: Anyone can say "crowded train". Only you saw the man reading over your shoulder.
tryPrompt: Picture one place you were today. Name one small thing there that nobody else would mention.
credit: Chip & Dan Heath, Made to Stick (Concrete)

title: One sharp detail is enough
rule: Pick the one detail that matters most, and leave the rest out.

examples.work: The meeting room was so cold that the client kept his jacket on the whole time.
examples.everyday: My friend's new flat is so small that the fridge is in the bedroom.

insteadOf: It was a big blue room with nine chairs, a whiteboard, two plants and a clock.
analogy: One green chilli lifts the dish. Ten ruin it.
tryPrompt: Describe where you are right now in one sentence, using only the one detail that stands out.

title: Name the person
rule: Give people names, or a short label, instead of "someone".

examples.work: Rahul from the data team asked me why repeat users had dropped.
examples.everyday: Mrs Joseph from the second floor asked if I could fix her Wi-Fi.

insteadOf: Someone from another team asked me something in the meeting.
analogy: In commentary, "a batter hit a six" is dull. "Kohli hit a six" makes you look up.
tryPrompt: Think of today's moment. Who was in it? Say their name, or a two-word label like "our intern".

title: Name the place
rule: Say exactly where it happened, so the listener can picture it.

examples.work: We were in the third-floor pantry, waiting for the coffee machine, when the fire alarm went off.
examples.everyday: We were stuck at the Hebbal junction when my sister called to say she'd passed her driving test.

insteadOf: We were somewhere in the office when it happened.
analogy: A film always shows you the street before the scene starts.
tryPrompt: Say where today's moment happened in under ten words, as exactly as you can.

title: Name the time
rule: An exact time, like "9:58", makes a moment feel real.

examples.work: At 8:47, the server went down. Our biggest client was due to log in at nine.
examples.everyday: At 11:15 p.m., the doorbell rang. It was my cousin, with a suitcase and no warning.

insteadOf: In the morning, the server went down before the client logged in.
analogy: A station announcement says "7:42", not "sometime in the evening".
tryPrompt: Start your moment from today with the exact time it happened, like "At 4:15…".

title: No name? Use a short label
rule: If you can't name someone, give them a short, clear label.

examples.work: The man from accounts who never speaks fixed the projector in ten seconds.
examples.everyday: The chai-wala outside the metro remembers my order better than my mother does.

insteadOf: This one person, some guy, I don't know who, he came and said…
analogy: Like a contact saved as "Plumber Raju": two words and you know exactly who.
tryPrompt: Think of someone in your day whose name you don't know. Give them a three-word label.

title: Who, where, when: one line
rule: Put the who, where and when in your first line, then move on.

examples.work: On Monday at ten, in the big conference room, Arjun deleted the wrong file in front of the client.
examples.everyday: Last Sunday at Juhu beach, my nephew buried my phone in the sand.

insteadOf: So there is this colleague, I'll tell you about him, he works in… anyway.
analogy: Like a ticket: date, time, seat. Then you go in and watch.
tryPrompt: Say a first line for today's moment with a who, a where and a when, in ten to fifteen words.

title: Quote one line
rule: Say one line exactly as the person said it, instead of reporting it.

examples.work: He leaned back and said, "Is this the final version?"
examples.everyday: My mother looked at my plate and said, "Only two rotis? What happened?"

insteadOf: He said that he wasn't happy with the deck.
analogy: A replay of the shot beats the commentator describing it.
tryPrompt: Think of one thing someone said to you today. Say it in their exact words.

title: Drop "that" before a quote
rule: Quote people directly: drop "that" and use their own words.

examples.work: My manager said, "Can you send it by five?"
examples.everyday: My brother texted, "Bring snacks. Don't ask why."

insteadOf: She said that "I am busy, call later."
analogy: A quote is a photocopy: the same words, nothing changed.
tryPrompt: Turn this into a direct quote: "She said that she would call me back."

title: Short lines hit harder
rule: Quote the short line that matters, not the whole conversation.

examples.work: He read my plan, put it down and said, "Who wrote this?"
examples.everyday: I showed my dad my new phone. He turned it over and asked, "Where's the headphone hole?"

insteadOf: He said a lot, about the numbers, the timeline, the team and the design…
analogy: The Bollywood dialogue everyone remembers is one line, not a speech.
tryPrompt: From one chat today, pick the single line that mattered most. Say just that line, in quotes.

title: Your own line counts too
rule: Quote your own words too, so we hear how you reacted.

examples.work: I said, "Give me ten minutes. I'll fix it before the client joins."
examples.everyday: I said, "Amma, I'm thirty. I can cross the road." She held my hand anyway.

insteadOf: I told him I would fix it soon.
analogy: A phone call has two voices. Let us hear yours too.
tryPrompt: Tell one moment from today with one line someone said and one line you said back.

title: Let the line show the mood
rule: Let what someone said show their mood, instead of naming it.

examples.work: The client typed in all caps: "WHO APPROVED THIS?"
examples.everyday: My sister texted, "Fine. Do whatever you want." Then nothing for two days.

insteadOf: The client was angry about the change.
analogy: You know your mother is upset from "Fine, beta." She doesn't need to say it.
tryPrompt: Think of someone who was annoyed or happy today. Say one line they said that shows it.

title: Show it through the body
rule: Instead of naming a feeling, say what your body did.

examples.work: Before the presentation, my hand was shaking so hard that the clicker rattled.
examples.everyday: When the results came out, my mouth went dry and I couldn't open the link.

insteadOf: I was very nervous before the presentation.
analogy: Actors don't say "I'm scared". Their hands shake, and we know.
tryPrompt: Think of a moment you were nervous. What did your hands, voice or stomach do? Say that.

title: Show it through what you did
rule: Say what you did when you felt it, and let us guess the feeling.

examples.work: I closed my laptop, walked to the pantry and made a second chai I didn't want.
examples.everyday: When India won, I ran out onto the balcony and shouted at nobody.

insteadOf: I was really angry with the vendor.
analogy: You know Dad's happy when he starts humming old songs while cooking.
tryPrompt: Pick one feeling from today. Without naming it, say one thing you did because of it.

title: Pick one sense
rule: Add one thing you heard, smelled, saw, tasted or felt.

examples.work: All morning, three phones kept ringing on the empty desk next to mine.
examples.everyday: The house smelled of ghee and cardamom, so I knew Amma was making Diwali sweets.

insteadOf: The office was busy in the morning.
analogy: Like the smell of wet earth before rain: one sense, and you're there.
tryPrompt: Think of one moment from today. What did you hear? Add that one sound to the story.

title: Keep feelings true-size
rule: Describe the feeling at its real size; don't blow it up.

examples.work: When the VP said my name, my ears went hot and I forgot my first line.
examples.everyday: When the waiter brought out the wrong cake, my friend and I just stared at each other.

insteadOf: I literally died. It was the worst moment of my whole life.
analogy: A tight single can be thrilling. Not every ball needs to be a six.
tryPrompt: Tell an embarrassing moment without "worst", "died" or "literally". Show one real body detail instead.

title: One body detail, then move on
rule: One body detail is enough; then get back to what happened.

examples.work: My hands were shaking as I clicked "Share screen". The wrong file opened.
examples.everyday: My heart was pounding as I knocked on the principal's door. He opened it, holding my old exam paper.

insteadOf: My hands shook, my heart raced, I was sweating, my legs were like jelly…
analogy: A pinch of hing flavours the whole dal. A spoonful ruins it.
tryPrompt: Tell today's moment with exactly one body detail. Then keep going with what happened next.

title: Cut three boring sentences
rule: Drop the first three sentences of setup and see if it still works.

examples.work: Halfway through my review, the CEO walked in and took the seat next to me.
examples.everyday: Halfway up the hill, my scooter ran out of petrol, and the nearest pump was three kilometres away.

insteadOf: I woke up, had chai, took the bus, reached office, opened my laptop, and then…
analogy: Like skipping the ads before a YouTube video. Nobody misses them.
tryPrompt: Tell today's moment. Then tell it again, starting three sentences later.

title: Short sentences at the tense bit
rule: When the moment gets tense, use short sentences.

examples.work: He reads my report. He reads it again. Then he looks up and says, "Did you check these numbers?"
examples.everyday: The ball went up. Everyone went quiet. My cousin, who never catches anything, held on.

insteadOf: He read my report and then he said that it was wrong.
analogy: In the last over, the commentary turns into short, sharp words.
tryPrompt: Find the tense second in today's moment. Tell just that part in sentences of five words or fewer.

title: One action per sentence
rule: At the key moment, give each action its own sentence.

examples.work: He opened my file. He scrolled. He stopped. He took off his glasses.
examples.everyday: My nephew took the last laddoo. He looked at me. He looked at his mother. He put it back.

insteadOf: He opened the file and scrolled and stopped and took off his glasses.
analogy: Like dealing cards one at a time, instead of dropping the whole pack.
tryPrompt: Take one tense moment from your week. Split it into four short sentences, one action each.

title: Skip what we can guess
rule: Skip the steps the listener can guess and jump to what's new.

examples.work: I opened the shared deck, and every slide I'd made had disappeared.
examples.everyday: By the time my cab reached the station, my train was pulling out.

insteadOf: I opened my laptop, logged in, opened my email, clicked the link, opened the deck…
analogy: Films cut from the hero leaving home to him arriving. Nobody needs the traffic.
tryPrompt: Tell today's moment and cut every step the listener could guess. What's left?

title: Don't explain the funny bit
rule: When the funny line lands, stop; explaining it kills the laugh.

examples.work: Forty minutes into a client call, I'm sure I'm on mute, so I tell my wife, "Make the paneer." Silence. Then their CFO unmutes: "Butter or kadai?"
examples.everyday: My grandmother asked Alexa to play old songs. Alexa said, "Sorry, I didn't get that." Nani said, "Nobody does, beta."

insteadOf: …and he asked which paneer. Get it? Because he heard me. So it was funny.
analogy: Explaining a joke is like explaining a magic trick: the magic goes.
tryPrompt: Tell a funny moment from this week. Stop the second the funny line is out. Don't add a word.
